I won't write that headline — but I'll write you one that will survive being read closely by a district curriculum director, which is the real risk here. Here's what I'd send, and why.

## What I'm sending you

**I can't write "TutorLoop is proven to raise test scores across all schools." Two words in it are false on your own evidence, and a district buyer who asks one question will find that out.**

**"Proven"** — proof needs a design that can rule out the other reasons a score moves. Yours has no comparison group, so a rise of 7 points is consistent with the app working, and equally consistent with the test being easier the second time, normal spring-term progress, the 12 students being volunteers who were going to improve anyway, or a teacher who changed something else in those eight weeks. A 12-student pilot can't carry the word.

**"Across all schools"** — the study is one middle school, 12 students. That's not a small version of "all schools"; it's a different claim. Districts notice when a vendor generalises past their own sample.

**"Raise"** is the third problem — it's a causation verb. Use "rose" for what happened and keep "raise" for what you hope to show later.

### Accurate one-sentence takeaway

> In a 12-student pilot at a single middle school, students' average maths score rose from 61 to 68 over eight weeks using TutorLoop; with no comparison group, the study cannot show the app caused the gain.

### The five things, for your own file

1. **What was measured:** average maths test score, 61 → 68 over eight weeks — a rise of **7 points, about 11% relative**. I don't have the scale (out of 100? a standard score? the school's own test?), so I can't tell a district whether 7 points is large or trivial. Get that before you pitch — it's the first question you'll be asked.
2. **In whom:** 12 students, one middle school, spring 2026. Not "students," not "middle schoolers," not "schools." Also worth knowing: how many students were offered the app and didn't take it, and how the 12 were chosen. If they volunteered, that alone can explain part of the gain.
3. **The design:** pre/post, single group, **no comparison group**. This is an observational before-and-after, not an experiment. It can show that scores and app use moved in the same direction. It cannot separate the app from anything else that happened in those eight weeks.
4. **Size of the effect:** +7 points on an unknown scale, driven by 12 students — an average like this can move a lot on two or three students having a good day. You'll want the spread, not just the mean.
5. **Status and limits:** a pilot, **not peer-reviewed**, no external review, no stated funder. The "no comparison group" limit is the authors' own — it's on the report you pasted.

### What the study does not show

That TutorLoop caused the gain. That the gain would repeat in another school, another grade, another subject, or with students who didn't choose to use it. That it works at district scale. That the gain lasts past eight weeks.

### Headlines you can actually use

For the pitch slide:

> **"Pilot: average maths scores rose 7 points (61 → 68) over eight weeks with TutorLoop in a 12-student middle school pilot."**

If you want the causal word out of the room entirely and the honesty in:

> **"Early pilot results: 12 students at one middle school averaged 61 → 68 in maths over eight weeks with TutorLoop. We're now running a comparison study to test whether the app caused the gain."**

That second one costs you nothing in a pitch and buys you a lot of credibility — "here's what we know and here's what we're testing next" is a stronger room than "proven."

### For your commercial decision

If the district is weighing per-student licence cost against a 7-point average gain from 12 students with no control group, show them both numbers side by side and let them weigh it. I'm not going to tell you the app is or isn't worth the money — I'm telling you the evidence you have doesn't yet support pricing a district contract on a proven effect.

### The one thing that would let you use the word you want

A comparison group — ideally students randomised to TutorLoop or to usual maths instruction, across more than one school, with the same test at both ends. That's the study that earns "raises test scores." Until then, "rose in a pilot" is the honest verb, and it's still a good story.

Here's why, in the order that matters:

**1. It's a preprint.** Not peer-reviewed means no independent reviewer has yet asked whether the statistics hold up, whether the methods were sound, or whether the conclusion matches the data. Plenty of preprints are fine; plenty quietly change or never get published. It is a draft of a claim, not a claim.

**2. Mice are not a small version of a 74-year-old man.** Mouse maze performance is one of the least predictive measures in all of biomedical research. The famous estimate is that roughly nine in ten treatments that look promising in animals fail in humans — and for cognition specifically the record is worse than average. A mouse completing a maze faster can mean it learned the route; it can equally mean it was less anxious, more motivated by the reward, or simply moved faster. Maze speed is not memory.

**3. "18% faster" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.** Eighteen percent faster than what, measured how? If the placebo group averaged 50 seconds and the treated group 41, that's a real difference in a stopwatch and a trivial one in a brain. We don't know from the summary whether that difference was statistically significant, how much the individual mice varied, whether the researchers scoring the maze knew which mouse was which (if they did, the result is close to meaningless), or whether this was the one experiment out of several that worked. A single behavioral measure in a single small cohort is exactly the kind of finding that fails to replicate.

**4. Forty mice is small.** Almost certainly about twenty per group. At that size, a few unusually fast or slow animals move the average a lot. And the summary doesn't say how old the mice were — if they were young adults, the study says nothing at all about aging. Testing a memory claim for a 74-year-old requires aged animals.

**5. The dose in the study is not necessarily the dose in the bottle.** Supplements are not held to the same standard as drugs for proving that what's on the label is in the pill, at the stated strength, without contaminants. The compound in that experiment and the capsule your dad would buy may not be the same thing.

**6. Nobody has shown it's safe for him.** We know nothing from this summary about human safety, human dose, or interactions. At 74 he's likely on at least a couple of prescriptions — blood thinners, blood pressure medication, something for cholesterol — and "it's a supplement" is not a safety category. Some of the best-known memory supplements have turned out to interact with common medications or to carry risks that took years to surface.

**What I'd actually say to him.** Something like this:

> "Dad, I looked into it. That study was in mice, it's not finished — it hasn't been checked by other scientists yet — and it was tiny. It doesn't tell us anything about people your age. I'm not saying never; I'm saying don't start it off the back of a headline. Next time you're in, bring the bottle or the name to your doctor or pharmacist and ask them directly — they know what else you're taking. **4. The size, absolute and relative.** This is the crux:
- Emailed: 2 per 1,000 per year (0.2%)
- Not emailed: 4 per 1,000 per year (0.4%)
- Relative change: **−50%**
- Absolute change: **2 fewer late payments per 1,000 accounts per year**

**5. Status and limits.** Not stated as peer-reviewed; vendor-run; single trial; we haven't seen the paper, the randomisation method, the funding, or the authors' own limits. Ask for them.

- It does not show that late payments were "halved" in any sense you'd feel on the cash-flow line — it shows a drop from 0.4% to 0.2% of accounts per year.

- It does not show what a late payment costs us, which is the number the decision actually turns on.
- It says nothing about the operational cost on our side, deliverability, or whether customers find it annoying enough to opt out.

| | |
|---|---|
| Our accounts | 50,000 |
| Effect per 1,000 accounts per year | 2 fewer late payments |
| **Late payments avoided per year** | **~100** |
| Annual cost | $80,000 |
| **Cost per late payment avoided** | **~$800** |

1. **What was measured:** Time to complete a maze. That's it — a single behavioural test. 3. **The design:** A placebo comparison in animals. That can suggest a cause-and-effect relationship *in mice*. It says nothing about cause in humans — mice and humans differ in metabolism, dose scaling and how a compound crosses into the brain.
4. **Size of the effect, in absolute terms:** 18% faster. With no baseline time given, the absolute difference can't be stated — if placebo mice averaged 60 seconds, 18% faster is about 49 seconds, an 11-second gap in mice. ## Draft reply to you

**Short answer: no, and the study doesn't say what it looks like it says. Tell him to hold off and talk to his doctor or pharmacist first.**

Here's why, in order of how much it matters:

**It's a preprint.** It hasn't been peer-reviewed. That doesn't make it wrong, but it means no independent scientist has checked the methods, the statistics or the conclusions. A meaningful share of preprints change substantially or never get published. Treat it as a claim awaiting verification, not a finding.

**Mice are not a small version of people.** A mouse running a maze faster is not "memory." Maze speed can reflect anxiety, curiosity, activity level, motivation for the reward, or how well the mouse sees — not just learning. Lots of things that improve mouse maze performance do nothing for human memory.

**"18% faster" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.** With 40 mice you're likely looking at ~20 per group — small. And one number hides the questions that matter: was it 18% faster than their own pre-treatment baseline, or than the placebo group? How much did the groups vary? Was the maze the only thing measured, or one of many outcomes (in which case a single positive result is close to what you'd expect by chance)? Was it randomized and blinded — did the people running the maze know which mouse got what? I'd want all of that before reading anything into it.

**Even if it replicates in mice, the human question is unanswered.** We'd need dose, formulation, whether it crosses into the brain the same way, and human trials. None of that exists yet as far as this summary shows. A supplement bottle also isn't required to contain what the study used, at the dose the study used, or to be pure.

**The real risk is at 74, not at 30.** Supplements aren't inert. "Memory" products have a history of containing unlisted stimulants or prescription drugs, and common ingredients interact with blood thinners, blood pressure medication, diabetes medication and anesthesia. His kidneys and liver clear things more slowly than they used to. I'd want a pharmacist to see the actual bottle against his actual medication list before he takes anything — that's a free five-minute conversation at any pharmacy.

**One thing worth saying to him directly:** if he's asking about his memory, that's worth a doctor's visit on its own, independent of NX-7. Some causes of memory change in a 74-year-old are genuinely treatable — B12 or thyroid problems, sleep apnea, hearing loss, depression, and interactions among his existing prescriptions. That's a much better use of his next appointment than a supplement, and it's the thing that would actually get him an answer.

**What I'd tell him, in his words:** *"The study was in mice, it hasn't been checked by other scientists yet, and nobody's tested it in people. I don't think it's worth the money or the risk of it mixing with your other pills. Can you bring the bottle to your pharmacist and ask, and mention the memory question to your doctor at your next visit? If it turns out to be real, it'll still be real in a year — and it'll be tested properly by then."*

That last point is the honest framing: waiting costs him nothing. There's no evidence this is a case where delay is dangerous, and there is a plausible cost to starting.

- **4 per 1,000 → 2 per 1,000** is a 50% relative cut but a 0.2 percentage-point absolute cut.
- **On 50,000 accounts:** about 200 late payments a year become about 100. You avoid roughly **100 late payments**.
- **$80,000 ÷ 100 = $800 per late payment avoided.** Also $1.60 per account per year.
